title: Issues: which product, which heading, which role
blurb: Decide whether issue information belongs in the issue management approach, issue register, issue report or daily log, and match each issue action to the right role.
question: At Calderbrook Borough Council, the project manager has assessed a request to add carers' visitor vouchers and needs to set out its impact on the baseline and recommend a decision. Which product should she use, and which board role decides with a focus on benefits?

teach.h: Three issue products and a diary
teach.body: Formally, the issue management approach (in the PID) describes how issues will be captured and reported and how changes to the baseline will be assessed and controlled. The issue register (in the project log) captures and maintains formal issues. An issue report describes an issue's impact on the baseline, identifies options and recommends a decision. In plain English: rules, list, and a decision paper. Informal or sensitive issues go in the project manager's daily log instead.

teach.caption: Old 6th edition name for the approach: change control approach. In PRINCE2 7, issue management includes change control (10.1).

children.label: Issue register
children.sub: Plus an issue report if a formal decision is needed

children.label: Risk register
children.sub: It is a risk, not an issue

head: Type
Signal in the scenario
rows: A proposal to change a baseline: 'can we add...'
A product does not or will not meet its quality specifications
Something has gone wrong now, with a negative impact
Timing and impact still need to be assessed
Something outside the project that may affect it
An unexpected positive consequence for the project or user organization
teach.caption: Issue types (10.1, 10.2.2, 10.2.3). A concession is an off-specification accepted without corrective action.

head: Role
Area of focus
rows: Ultimate authority for changes; may delegate
Runs issue and change procedures; corrective action
Implements corrective actions in the work package
Manages one issue through to resolution
teach.caption: Table 10.2 and 10.2.4. If there is no project support, the project manager maintains the register.

teach.h: The issue technique, with who does it

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: PM via work packages; TM does it

teach.caption: Capture, assess, recommend, decide, implement (10.3.1).

teach.h: Issue owner, project manager, change authority
teach.body: Three near-miss roles. The issue owner looks after one issue until it is resolved. The project manager runs the issue and change control procedure for the whole project, assisted by project support. A change authority is a person or group to whom the board delegates authority to approve requests for change and off-specifications, within limits and usually with a change budget. The board stays the ultimate authority, and the delegation is written into the issue management approach.

In the private beta, senior user Ruth Abernethy asks for carers' visitor vouchers to be added online: a request for change. Project support registers it, with Ruth as issue owner. Hannah Okoro assesses it with Kestrel Lane's Tom Achebe (three sprints, £45,000) and writes an issue report. The board has delegated changes up to £10,000 to Hannah, so this goes to the board, where Ruth focuses on safeguarding benefits. Once approved, Hannah amends the product description and work package; Tom's team builds it.

rows.label: Changes over £10,000 go to the project board
Carers' vouchers request: owner Ruth; status open
Approve for £45,000, or defer until after go-live
An officer privately says two colleagues may resign
The health check may fail in the public beta

teach.text: Traps: (1) the issue owner manages one issue; the project manager runs the issue and change control procedure; (2) a change authority only approves within delegated limits; the board is the ultimate authority; (3) an issue within tolerance needs an issue report, not an exception report; (4) sensitive issues go in the daily log, not the open issue register.

items: Issue management approach (PID): how issues and changes are captured, assessed and controlled.
Issue register (project log): formal issues, with type, owner and status; close once resolved.
Issue report: impact on the baseline, options and a recommended decision.
Senior user decides escalated issues with a focus on benefits; PM runs the procedure; TM implements.
Project support maintains the register; with no support, the PM does it.

summary: You can now decide whether issue information belongs in the issue management approach, issue register, issue report or daily log, and name the issue type. You can also match issue actions to the board, senior user, change authority, project manager, team manager, project support and issue owner.

A.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is in the private beta stage. The board approved a request to rework the address lookup screen. Project manager Hannah Okoro has already updated the product description and issued an amended work package to Kestrel Lane Digital. Which role should now implement the corrective action within the work package?
A.why: The team manager implements corrective actions within the work package; the PM's part was to create the updated product description and work package (table 10.2).

whyNot.0: The PM has already done their part by amending the product description and work package.
whyNot.2: Project support maintains the issue register; it does not build products.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier commits supplier resources and is accountable for supplier quality, but does not carry out the work package.

A.q: Tarnside College's Engineering Skills Centre project is in the detailed design stage. The vice principal for curriculum has asked for 30 welding bays instead of 24. Project manager Leah Whitfield assesses it at about £60,000 and one week, within stage tolerances, and identifies two options. Which product should she use to set out the impact on the baseline and recommend a decision?
A.why: An issue report describes an issue's impact on the baseline, identifies options and recommends a decision; it is used for requests for change needing formal review (10.5).

whyNot.0: An exception report is for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance; this change is within tolerance.
whyNot.1: A highlight report summarizes stage status for the board at agreed intervals; it is not a decision paper for one change.
whyNot.2: The register entry records and tracks the issue, but does not set out options and a recommendation.

A.q: Fernhollow Kitchen has a project support officer. The Harbridge's buyer has just asked for a change to the sleeve design, and it must be recorded so that it can be tracked through change control. Which role should record it in the issue register?
A.why: Project support administers the issue and change control procedure by maintaining the issue register (table 10.2).

whyNot.1: Project assurance checks on the board's behalf and is kept separate from project support's administration.
whyNot.2: Team managers implement corrective actions in their work packages; they do not keep the project's register.
whyNot.3: A change authority decides on requests within its limits; it does not record them.

B.q: Calderbrook's project board is considering an escalated request to add carers' visitor vouchers to the online service. The change would cost £45,000 and is beyond the project manager's delegated authority. Which board role should decide with a particular focus on safeguarding the expected benefits?
B.why: The senior user makes decisions on escalated issues with particular focus on safeguarding the expected benefits (table 10.2).

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case and is accountable overall, but the benefits focus on escalated issues is the senior user's.
whyNot.1: The senior supplier's focus is on supplier resources, quality and technical integrity.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board; it does not make decisions on escalated issues.

B.q: Wenmoor Community Health's single point of access project is in the pilot stage. Senior district nurse Gareth Pugh tells project manager Ellie Chandran privately that several Moorside nurses have said they will refuse the new rotas. He asks her not to share his name. Where should Ellie record this?
options: In the daily log, as an informal issue
In the issue register, as a formal concern
In the risk register, as a threat
In the lessons log, as a lesson
B.why: Informal issues, and sensitive matters where open access would be inappropriate, are recorded in the daily log rather than the issue register (11.5).

whyNot.1: The issue register is an open record of formal issues, which is unsuitable for a sensitive, confidential report.
whyNot.2: The nurses have already stated their position, so this is a current issue, and the risk register is an open record unsuited to a confidential report.
whyNot.3: Nothing has been learned for future work yet; it is a sensitive issue to handle now.

B.q: Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline is in initiation. The board decides to delegate approval of requests for change up to £25,000 each to a change authority of the project manager and the enterprise architect, with a change budget of £150,000. Where should this delegation be documented?
B.why: The issue management approach describes how changes to the baseline will be controlled, including delegated change authority and change budget use (10.5, 10.2.4).

whyNot.0: The risk management approach covers risk procedures and the risk budget, not change authority.
whyNot.1: The register records individual issues, not the rules for approving changes.
whyNot.2: The communication management approach covers who receives what information and when, not approval limits.

C.q: Carrowford's half marathon project is in planning and approvals. Project manager Kezia Oduya makes Lisa Ventnor, Paceline's race director, the issue owner for a problem with the timing chip supplier. Because Lisa is very experienced, Kezia also hands her the running of the issue and change control procedure for the whole project. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because Lisa has more event experience than Kezia
Yes, because an issue owner is allocated to each issue
No, because the PM runs issue and change control
No, because issue owners must sit on the project board
C.why: The project manager manages the issue and change control procedures, assisted by project support; an issue owner looks after a single issue (table 10.2).

whyNot.0: Experience makes Lisa a good issue owner, but it does not move the PM's responsibility for the procedure.
whyNot.1: Each issue does have an owner, but that does not explain handing over the whole procedure.
whyNot.3: Issue owners need not be board members; the problem is giving away the PM's procedure.

C.q: On Calderbrook's project, the request for carers' visitor vouchers was approved, the product description updated and the work completed in sprint 9. The project support officer leaves the issue marked 'open' in the issue register until the end of the project, so the board can see it at closure. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the board should see all issues at closure
Yes, because open issues need follow-on actions at closure
No, because it has been decided and implemented
No, because the change authority sets each issue's status
C.why: An issue that has received management consideration and whose change has been implemented should be closed in the register (10.1, 10.5).

whyNot.0: The register keeps the history of closed issues, so leaving it open does not help the board.
whyNot.1: Follow-on actions are for issues still open at closure; this one has been resolved.
whyNot.3: The change authority decides on requests; updating issue status is part of maintaining the register.

C.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in its trials stage. The colour on the first 5,000 printed sleeves is slightly outside the agreed specification, and Harbridge's buyer is content to accept them. After reviewing an issue report, the project board, which has not delegated any change authority, accepts the sleeves without any rework. Is this an appropriate application of the issues practice, and why?
options: Yes, because it can be accepted as a concession
Yes, because a quality problem is a request for change
No, because off-specifications go in the quality register
No, because the supplier must correct every faulty item
C.why: An off-specification may be accepted without corrective action as a concession, by the board or a change authority with the right authority (10.3.1.4, table 10.1).

whyNot.1: Sleeves that miss their specification are an off-specification, not a request for change.
whyNot.2: Off-specifications are issues handled through change control and the issue register.
whyNot.3: Granting a concession is a valid decision for an off-specification, so rework is not required.

reteach.title: A busy restaurant
reteach.question: A restaurant has house rules for complaints, a complaints book, a note to the owner about a big refund and the manager's private notebook. Which is which in PRINCE2?

blocks.body: The house rules say how complaints are logged, rated and who can approve refunds up to what value: the issue management approach. The complaints book lists every formal complaint with who is handling it and its status: the issue register. A note to the owner setting out a large refund, the options and a recommendation is an issue report. A waiter's private worry about a colleague goes in the manager's notebook: the daily log.

blocks.text: The person handling one complaint (issue owner) is not the person who runs the whole complaints system (project manager).

explain.body: Request for change proposes a change to a baseline. Off-specification is a product that will not meet its specification. Problem and concern are other issues needing attention.

test.q: On Calderbrook's project, the first batch of permit records migrated from the old database fails its agreed data quality check: 2% are missing vehicle registrations against a limit of 0.5%. Which type of issue is this?
test.why: An off-specification is a product that does not or will not meet its quality specifications (10.2.3).

whyNot.0: Nobody is proposing a change to a baseline; a delivered product misses its specification.
whyNot.1: It is negative and current, but the specific type for a product failing its specification is off-specification.
whyNot.2: A concern needs its timing and impact assessed; here a product has clearly failed its specification.

explain.body: The issue management approach sets the rules: how issues are captured and reported, priority and severity scales, version control, delegated change authority and how the change budget is used.

test.q: During initiation of Tarnside College's project, project manager Leah Whitfield wants to define the scales that everyone will use to rate the priority and severity of issues. Where should these scales be recorded?
test.why: Priority and severity scales are part of how issues are captured and assessed, so they belong in the issue management approach (10.5).

whyNot.0: The register records individual issues, rated using the scales defined elsewhere.
whyNot.2: The quality management approach covers quality procedures and responsibilities, not issue scales.
whyNot.3: The daily log is the PM's informal diary.

explain.body: After a change is approved, the project manager implements it by creating or updating product descriptions and work packages. The team manager then does the work.

test.q: Wenmoor Community Health's board approves adding a carer referral form to the new service. Which role should create the product description for the new form and amend the work package?
test.why: The project manager implements corrective actions, for example creating product descriptions and work packages for agreed extra scope (table 10.2).

whyNot.0: The senior supplier commits supplier resources; the PM prepares work packages.
whyNot.1: The team manager implements the work within the work package once the PM has issued it.
whyNot.3: Project assurance gives independent advice to the board; it does not prepare work packages.

explain.body: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and off-specifications. It may delegate to a change authority or the project manager; if it has not, it decides itself.

test.q: Carrowford's project board has not delegated any change authority. Paceline Events asks to move part of the route, which would change the certified course in the project's baseline. Who should decide on this request for change?
test.why: The project board is the ultimate authority for requests for change and decides them itself unless it has delegated authority (10.2.4).

whyNot.1: The PM may approve changes only where the board has delegated that authority.
whyNot.2: The race director may raise or own the issue but cannot approve a change to the baseline.
whyNot.3: Project assurance advises the board; it does not approve changes.
